Abstract 7

This systematic and large-scale reproduction effort tests the reproducibility and 8

robustness of economics and political science, contributing to a growing literature 9

on research credibility and self-correction in science [1–4]. We reproduced origi- 10

nal analyses and conducted robustness checks of 110 articles recently published 11

in leading economics and political science journals, all of which have mandatory 12

data and code sharing policies [17,18]. We found that over 85% of published 13

claims were computationally reproducible. In robustness checks, our re-analyses 14

led to 72% of statistically significant estimates to remain significant and in the 15

same direction, and the median reproduced effect size is (nearly) the same as the 16

originally published effect size (that is, 99% of the published effect size). Addition- 17

ally, six independent research teams examined 12 pre-specified hypotheses about 18

determinants of robustness. Research teams with more experience found lower 19

levels of robustness, and robustness correlated with neither author characteristics 20

nor data availability. 21

1 Introduction 22

Science aspires to be cumulative. Reproducibility efforts strengthen science by testing 23

the reliability of published findings, promoting self-correction, and informing policy- 24

making [1]. Computational reproductions, whereby independent researchers reproduce 25

the results of published studies, are an essential diagnostic tool [2–10]. Such efforts 26

should have greater visibility [11–16]. However, there has been little social science 27

reproduction and robustness conducted at scale [10, 13, 17–23]. 28

This project is a mega-reproduction led by the Institute for Replication (I4R), 29

which evaluates the reproducibility and robustness of 110 published studies in eco- 30

nomics (79) and political science (31). Our focus is on studies published in 12 31

prestigious journals between 2022 and 2023. While each of these journals has a data 32

and code availability policy requiring authors to publicly share their materials upon 33

publication, most (though not all) also appoint a dedicated data editor. This edi- 34

tor is responsible for enforcing the journal’s data and code policy and conducting 35

internal computational reproducibility checks for accepted studies (see Supplementary 36

Materials 11.5). 37

Not all studies from our targeted journals were chosen for reproduction and 38

robustness, and our sample is thus not a random representative sample of studies 39

in economics and political science. Our approach leads to an over-representation of 40

studies using publicly available data ([18]). Another feature of our sample is that the 41

targeted journals have a data availability policy and enforce it. This is in contrast to 42

many top field journals in both economics and political science. Our sample should 43

thus be viewed as very selective both in terms of impact and high data and code avail- 44

ability rates, and might present an optimistic upper bound on reproducibility rates. 45

In fact, virtually all papers in our sample include replication packages with cleaned 46

data and code to reproduce the paper’s results, and about 30% also provide the raw 47

data and cleaning code used to generate the analytical data (Extended Data Figure 48

1, Levels 8, 9, and 10). 49

While this project relates to the broader reproducibility movement in psychology, 50

neuroscience, or biomedicine, it distinguishes itself from notable social science repli- 51

cation efforts along four key dimensions [24–26]. First, we are mostly reproducing 52

(non-experimental) studies using the same data as the original authors. Second, we 53

assess computational reproducibility and test the robustness of estimates to alternative 54

specification choices. Because of the unique nature of the underlying studies–largely 55

non-experimental work that uses observational data–we offer the first evidence about 56

the general robustness of economics and political science. Third, we concentrate on 57

recent studies for both economics and political science. Finally, this is an ongoing 58

initiative that aims to expand across disciplines, with the goal of mass reproducing 59

studies and reshaping research norms at scale. This paper reports findings from the 60

first 110 reproductions. 61

2 Definitions 62

We follow [27]’s nomenclature and define a claim computationally reproducible if 63

its results can be reproduced using the original study’s data and protocols. A claim 64

is robust if its results are robust to alternative reasonable analytical decisions on the 65

same data. Last, a claim is replicable if its results can be repeated using new data. 66

3 Teams and Choice of Study 67

The reproductions and replications in this project are generated in one of two streams. 68

First, I4R has a board of editors who recommend potential reproducers. Second, I4R 69

held 11 events called replication games (Games) ([28]). Games are one-day events 70

open to faculty, post-docs, graduate students and other researchers. Participants are 71

assigned to a small team of about 3–5 other researchers all working in the same subfield 72

(e.g., development economics). 73

Participant teams are offered a short list of (average 5) studies in their subfield 74

of interest about three weeks before the games. They are asked to choose a paper as 75

a team, and familiarize themselves with the data and codes publicly posted by the 76

original authors (i.e., replication package) prior to the games. After the Game, teams 77

submit a standardized reproduction report summarizing their results. 78

I4R emphasizes to reproducers that the goal is not to show that the results are 79

not reproducible. The goal is instead to test if the claims are reproducible and robust. 80

This is key as some reproducers might engage in reverse specification searching (i.e., 81

selective reporting of insignificant results). I4R stresses the importance of reasonable 82

robustness checks and recoding [29]. Re-analyses are sensible tests of the research 83

question and expected to be statistically valid and theoretically informed. 84

We survey the reasons why teams selected their paper (Extended Data Figure 2). 85

While 13.6% of teams were assigned a study (i.e., did not choose which study to work 86

on), about 45% of teams report “Methods used”, 36% of teams selected “because of 87

the journal of publication” and about 25% due to the “length of time to reproduce 88

results”. 89

If a large portion of reproducers select papers based on the assumption that their 90

findings are questionable, it could skew reproducibility rates downward, as such studies 91

might be more prone to revealing problematic outcomes. However, in this project, 92

only a minimal fraction of teams indicated that they chose their paper because of ex 93

ante beliefs that main results are (not) replicable (3.6%). We found that selecting a 94

paper due to the reproducers’ belief the paper is not robust is inversely correlated 95

with reproducer experience (ρ = −0.19, p < 0.000). A few teams (5%) indicated that 96

their choice was based on statistical power/sample size and trust of original authors. 97

4 Data and Computational Reproducibility 98

We find a computational reproducibility rate of 85%. That is, when provided with 99

the original data and code, independent researchers are able to reproduce the pub- 100

lished results in economics and political science studies 85% of the time using either: 101

(1) the raw and analytical data, or; (2) the analytical data when the raw data were 102

not provided. The remaining 15% of cases involved studies with only partial availabil- 103

ity of code or data, or instances where code failed to run or produced inconsistent 104

results (See Supplementary Materials 11.8 and Extended Data Figure 1). Fixing paths, 105

missing packages and software requirements were not considered failures of computa- 106

tional reproducibility. In those instances, we fixed paths, added missing packaged and 107

software requirements. 108

Our findings suggest high rates of computationally reproducible results, but far 109

from perfect for leading journals. Our results are in contrast with several studies 110

documenting low computational reproducibility rates in economics [19]; [13]; [22]. This 111

may in part reflect the effectiveness of editorial policies in journals that have introduced 112

data editors and mandatory sharing of replication packages. 113

5 Robustness 122

For robustness, we directly compare original point estimates to the revised point esti- 123

mates. This one-on-one comparison allows us to speak to the robustness of a specific 124

hypothesis test, in addition to the robustness of our entire sample. We are thus looking 125

at several claims within a study and conduct robustness reproducibility and robustness 126

for multiple claims. 127

Reproducers are then free to conduct any robustness or recoding exercises. They 128

focus on the reproducibility of the claims and have access to the replication package, 129

allowing them to directly test the robustness of the main results. This is a crucial 130

advantage over the traditional review process as reproducers may uncover coding errors 131

and discrepancies between the paper and the codes. They may also uncover coding 132

decisions that were not discussed (or are hard to find) in the article. 133

However, this flexibility also brings some disadvantages. As with the journal review 134

process with reviewers, reproducers spend different amounts of time and effort on their 135

respective replication. Some reproducers are more experienced at coding, while others 136

are more familiar with methods, or simply unable to implement robustness checks due 137

to a lack of raw data (Extended Data Figure 7). This means that reproducibility efforts 138

and type of re-analysis vary across teams. Teams worked on average 13 active days 139

(std. dev. of 24) on the reproductions and robustness, and reports were on average 19 140

pages long (std. dev. of 14). 141

8 Coding Errors and Recoding 260

We investigate the prevalence of coding errors and discrepancies between the code 261

and article. Computational reproducibility pertains to the provided replication folder’s 262

ability to reproduce the exhibits and statistics displayed in the research (manuscripts, 263

appendices, etc.). Reproducers may be able to reproduce all exhibits exactly as they 264

appear (computationally reproducible), but the exhibits may have been constructed 265

with coding errors or discrepancies. 266

Except for minor inconveniences (i.e., missing packages or broken pathways), we 267

identify coding errors in approximately 25% of the studies, with some studies contain- 268

ing multiple errors (Supplementary Materials 11.10). The prevalence of coding errors is 269

larger for economics (26%) than political science (16%). Types of errors include: defin- 270

ing the dependent variable, defining the main independent variable, defining control 271

variables, mis-specification of the estimation/model, inference or the sample. While not 272

all of these coding errors impacted the conclusions of the original studies, we uncover 273

several significant errors that warrant discussion. These major errors include instances 274

of duplicated observations on a large scale, incomplete interaction in a difference-in- 275

differences model, mislabeling the main treatment variable for a substantial number 276

(or all) of observations, and using different models, or estimators, than reported in 277

the article. 278

It is important to note that this 25% figure likely underestimates the true preva- 279

lence of coding errors. Reproducers may have missed some errors, and many replication 280

packages do not include raw data or data-cleaning code, limiting the ability to detect 281

additional issues. 282

A number of reproducers also recoded the analysis using a different statistical 283

software. Out of 23 recoding exercises, we find major differences for three studies and 284

minor differences for 10 studies. Two of the major differences were uncovered when 285

using a different software and looking at the authors’ code. Additionally, one team who 286

computationally reproduced the results using a different version of the software used 287

by the authors uncovered noteworthy differences in the magnitude and significance of 288

the estimates (Supplementary Materials 11.9). 289

10 Discussion 309

A substantial information asymmetry exists between authors and the broader aca- 310

demic community, including reviewers and editors ([30]). Reviewers rarely see the 311

underlying data and code and may be unaware of crucial coding decisions, even as 312

journals routinely request multiple robustness checks. This limited visibility means 313

major errors or inconsistencies can go undetected. 314

Large-scale reproducibility initiatives offer a promising way to address these chal- 315

lenges in the social sciences and beyond. Our project provides a systematic, scalable 316

approach to evaluating reproducibility and robustness, with the goal of increasing 317

transparency and improving the credibility of published research. While stronger 318

incentives to conduct reproducibility and robustness remain necessary, we do not 319

attempt to evaluate which specific incentives would be most effective, as doing so 320

would require speculation beyond the scope of our data. Identifying the most effective 321

incentives is an important research question that we hope future work will address. 322

Given the low prevalence of diagnostic replication in published work [38], the 323

scale of this ongoing effort could shift research norms. By encouraging more rigorous 324

methodologies, deterring questionable research practices, and emphasizing collabo- 325

ration, it may help place greater weight on the reliability of results in publication 326

decisions. 327

Although our journal sample is selective, the findings are encouraging and suggest 328

a high level of computational reproducibility. These patterns—and the existence of a 329

large-scale, community-driven effort—may strengthen trust in published results. 330

We also asked reproducers about the quality of the replication packages they exam- 331

ined. Over 40% reported gaining a more optimistic view of the discipline, while only 332

about 5% developed a more negative opinion. This suggests that mass reproduction 333

of studies accompanied by replication packages can directly enhance researchers’ trust 334

in scientific findings. 335

By late 2025, I4R had organized 80 replication games involving over 3,500 researchers, 338

with events held every other week. These efforts show that the skilled labor needed for 339

large-scale reproduction can emerge organically from an engaged research community. 340

The project also has the potential to advance science and improve equity. Publicly 341

posting data and code facilitates learning, speeds methodological diffusion, and enables 342

independent verification. Reproducing analyses in open-source software can also help 343

level the playing field for researchers who lack access to expensive licenses. 344

Our results have limitations. Only a small number of economics and political 345

science journals currently require data and code [17]; [18], and even fewer check 346

reproducibility [39]. Thus, our findings largely reflect leading journals with strong 347

data-sharing norms. Future research should assess reproducibility more broadly by 348

examining a random sample of papers from journals with and without data availability 349
